#7276. GitLab: Principal Revenue Strategist

GitLab is the intelligent orchestration platform for DevSecOps. GitLab enables organizations to increase developer productivity, improve operational efficiency, reduce security and compliance risk, and accelerate digital transformation. More than 50 million registered users and more than 50% of the Fortune 100* trust GitLab to ship better, more secure software faster.

The same principles built into our products are reflected in how our team works: we embrace AI as a core productivity multiplier, with all team members expected to incorporate AI into their daily workflows to drive efficiency, innovation, and impact. GitLab is where careers accelerate, innovation flourishes, and every voice is valued. Our high-performance culture is driven by our values and continuous knowledge exchange, enabling our team members to reach their full potential while collaborating with industry leaders to solve complex problems. Co-create the future with us as we build technology that transforms how the world develops software.

*Fortune 500® is a registered trademark of Fortune Media IP Limited, used under license. Claim based on GitLab data. Fortune 100 refers to the top 20% ranked companies in the 2025 Fortune 500 list, published in June 2025. Fortune and Fortune Media IP Limited are not affiliated with, and do not endorse products or services of GitLab.

As a Principal Revenue Strategist, you'll help shape how GitLab brings its products to market as artificial intelligence changes how software is built and bought. Reporting to the VP of Revenue Strategy, you'll be a senior individual contributor connecting market, product, and field insights to clear recommendations and changes in how we sell. Google published new guidance for recognizing Google-Agent and allowing its agents to interact with websites securely.

Google published new guidance on how to keep from blocking its user-triggered AI agents that identify themselves as Google-Agent. The new documentation shows how to verify legitimate Google-Agent requests and configure firewalls to allow them on websites.

Google-Agent is the name used by AI agents hosted on Google’s infrastructure that navigate websites and perform actions on behalf of users. Google’s guidance and also Google’s User-Triggered Fetcher documentation do not identify which Google products or services use Google-Agent. Neither documentation mentions Google Search, AI Mode, Gemini, or any other Google product.

It describes Google-Agent as agents that are hosted on Google’s infrastructure, interact with and navigate websites, and complete tasks on behalf of a user.

The document says or implies that the Google-Agent does the following:

The new guidance explains there are three ways that website owners can verify that a request comes from Google-Agent.

1. The request’s User-Agent header contains “Google-Agent.”

2. The request originates from an IP address listed in Google’s published file of user-triggered agent ranges.

3. Only where it’s present, when the request carries a cryptographic signature under Google’s experimental Web Bot Auth protocol, which can be checked against Google’s published public keys.

The first two checks are the baseline, and the signature check adds stronger verification when it’s available. A Google-Agent bot can then be allowed through whatever bot defenses are in use once it passes those checks. Google also notes that some CDNs and bot-detection services handle this verification automatically.

Lastly, Google offers guidance on troubleshooting when the Google-Agent is unintentionally blocked.

Google recommends ensuring that rules allowing Google-Agent requests have higher priority and are evaluated before broader blocking rules, including:

If bot detection, firewall (WAF), or CDN rules only covers the initial page request, the agent will be able to land on the website but it will be unable to finish whatever task it’s there to accomplish.

Google recommends checking that CAPTCHA challenges are disabled for verified Google-Agent requests, reviewing rate limits, IP address updates, and proxy configurations.

“Proxy headers: Confirm that load balancers and intermediate proxies preserve the original client IP, the User-Agent header, and (for signed requests) the Signature, Signature-Input, and Signature-Agent headers.”

Google’s new guidance addresses three issues to check if Google-Agent is being inadvertently blocked:

“Shared-IP rate limits: Confirm that per-IP rate-limiting rules account for or exempt verified Google-Agent IP ranges, as concurrent requests from multiple users share the same egress pool.

IP range updates: Confirm that IP-based rules stay synced with the latest ranges in user-triggered-agents.json.

Proxy headers: Confirm that load balancers and intermediate proxies preserve the original client IP, the User-Agent header, and (for signed requests) the Signature, Signature-Input, and Signature-Agent headers.”

Google’s new Google-Agent guidance offers tips for website owners who want to allow Google-Agent interactions, stressing that they need to make sure that legitimate Google-Agent requests can pass through security defenses without compromising protections against unwanted bots.

#7271. The Final Ad Checklist Before BFCM – What To Fix Now & What To Leave via @sejournal, @tonyadam

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Keep Black Friday ads running with final checks on Google budget limits, Meta spend caps, purchase tracking, and offer consistency before Cyber Monday.

Your Black Friday advertising should now be built, paced, and approved. The useful work left is checking what’s running will continue running and being honest about anything that isn’t ready. Some of it can still be fixed in the few days before Black Friday on Nov. 27, and some of it belongs on next year’s plan.

This is the checklist our team works through on the accounts we run through the end of the holiday season. Most of this is dull stuff, sure, but the last thing you want is something like this breaking at the worst possible time. So think of it like our checklist being passed on to you to make sure that doesn’t happen.

If you have not built campaigns by now, you are really cutting it close and leaving it for last minute. For the accounts we run, the freeze date was last Friday, Nov. 20, and since then the only changes going in are fixes or tweaks. Any major changes now could trigger you right back into learning mode, and you don’t want that. Campaigns should be structured, stable, and running leading into Black Friday Cyber Monday (BFCM).

If something still isn’t built, only launch low-risk pieces, like a brand campaign if you somehow don’t have one, or promo creative inside an asset group or ad set that already has history. Anything structural goes on next year’s plan.

Pacing should have started in early November, so budgets are already close to where you want them on Black Friday instead of sitting at an October level waiting for one big jump on Thursday. Frankly speaking, most companies start their BFCM offers early, so if that’s you, you have nothing to worry about here because you might already be ramped up.

On Meta, the ramp should have happened in steps, since frequent budget changes can send ad sets back into learning. Meta’s developer documentation describes budget scheduling as a way to “schedule budget increases for your campaign or ad set budget” for days when you expect higher sales. If you scheduled increases, check the dates and amounts against your sale.

On Google, a campaign can spend up to twice its average daily budget on a given day, and no more than 30.4 times the average daily budget over the month. When you change a budget partway through the month, Google recalculates the monthly limit as what you’ve spent so far plus the new daily budget times the remaining calendar days, counting the day of the edit.

Cyber Monday 2026 falls on Nov. 30, the last day of the month, so if you raise a budget that morning, the monthly limit becomes what you’ve spent plus one day of the new budget, and you won’t be charged for more than that one day regardless of the 2x daily allowance. A campaign that runs close to double its budget Friday through Sunday is also using the monthly room Cyber Monday would have had. So treat Black Friday through Cyber Monday as one stretch, set those budgets before the weekend, and check on Sunday night how much monthly room your key campaigns have left.

Google’s campaign total budgets let you set one budget for a three- to 90-day window on Performance Max, Search, and Shopping, but they’re only available for new campaigns, so this isn’t the week to start using them. The monthly limit starts over on Dec. 1, so set December budgets now as well.

If budgets haven’t ramped, raise Google budgets today, since the change takes effect immediately and the rest of the month paces to the new number. On Meta, start stepping budgets up today rather than all at once on Thursday night. And write down the budget you wish you’d had on November 1, because that’s where next year’s ramp starts.

See also: Google Ads Channel Priorities Have Limits – What PMax Still Won’t Let You Split

A few things can’t be checked in a settings screen, so these are the questions I’d want an honest answer to before Thursday, and what I’d do if the answer is no.

Prospecting funded in September and October is what pays during BFCM. In our accounts, upper-funnel spend takes roughly six to eight weeks to show up in revenue, which is why I argued that September was the last month to fund it. Your own lag depends on price point and how long people take to decide.

If the answer is no: Don’t launch cold prospecting this week, when in our accounts prospecting CPMs are at their highest of the year. Keep the prospecting you have on a flat budget through the week and let harvest campaigns take the extra money. Put the build on next year’s calendar for September, as a fixed budget rather than a percentage of whatever is left.

It should lean towards Bottom Of Funnel (BoFu). BFCM is when the demand you built in the fall turns into orders, so retargeting, brand search, and your existing customers are going to take a bigger share of spend than they do the rest of the year. During the holidays, those sales are worth buying. What matters is that it was a decision. Before the week starts, you should know roughly how much budget is going to people who already know you, how much stays on new customers, and what the floor is for prospecting so it doesn’t get raided the first time retargeting looks great on Friday morning.

Keep in mind that during BFCM, your email, SMS, retargeting, and brand campaigns are often all reaching the same person for the same order, and each one will report it. So don’t move budget into retargeting just because its ROAS looks great on Black Friday. Check it against what the store is actually doing overall before you add more.

You can see the split on both platforms. On Google, lifecycle goal reporting adds a “New vs. returning customers” segment to the Campaigns table on campaigns where the new customer acquisition goal is turned on, and on Meta, audience segments break sales campaign results into new, engaged, and existing customers once you’ve defined them in your ad account settings.

If the answer is no: Decide it today. Write down the prospecting floor and the rough share for new versus existing customers through Cyber Monday, and look at the new versus returning numbers each morning so you’re adjusting against the plan instead of against whichever campaign has the best ROAS that day.

You should by now. Testing is what October is for, and BFCM is when you have winning creative you know you can put advertising dollars against. That matters most on Meta, where the creative is doing most of the targeting in Advantage+, so in our accounts, a proven concept with the offer added to it tends to beat a brand new idea during holiday shopping. The offer can go on as an overlay, in the first few seconds of a video, or in the headline, without changing what made the ad work in the first place.

If the answer is no: Look back at the last 60 to 90 days, pick the best performer on each platform by cost per purchase, and add the offer to that. Don’t run a creative test during the most expensive week of the year, because whatever wins under BFCM pricing won’t tell you much about January. Put an October testing window on next year’s plan, so you go into the holiday season with your winners already picked.

Every date through December should have creative approved and paused: Black Friday, Cyber Monday, any Cyber Week extension, shipping deadlines, last-minute gifts and gift cards, and post-Christmas on Dec. 26.

Google’s ad review page says most ads are reviewed within one business day and “changes to your ad or assets restart the review process and may cause delays.” Meta’s Marketing API best practices say changes to creative or targeting trigger review and that an ad entering review while paused stays paused after approval.

If the answer is no: Submit what’s missing today with final copy and schedule it with end dates, because Thanksgiving week is short on business days and a typo caught after approval means another trip through review.

Place a real order with your promo code and follow it into Google Ads and Meta Events Manager. A tag check only confirms that something fired, and a checkout change made in November can alter the value your purchase event sends without stopping it from firing.

If something is off, it’s worth pulling a developer in before Wednesday. If tracking breaks during the week anyway, fix it and apply a data exclusion so the bidder doesn’t learn from the broken days. Cancel the test order afterward.

The site banner, landing page, sale price in your feed, Merchant Center promotions, and ad copy should all say the same thing, because a mismatch usually shows up as disapprovals the morning the sale starts. Merchant Center’s automatic item updates are on by default and correct prices from your landing pages, but Google says they may not work for products whose price changes more than once a day.

Push your own feed updates for any hourly doorbusters, run a purchase on the promo landing page from a phone the way a customer would, and name the person who opens Merchant Center diagnostics first thing Black Friday.

Billing is the item most likely to stop every ad you have. Google says a declined payment can stop the account, and on monthly invoicing, once costs reach the account budget, “all ads in the account stop running.” On Meta, the ad account spend cap is a hard stop, and “when the amount is reached, all delivery stops.”

Raise the invoiced account budget to cover the higher spend through Nov. 30, reset any Meta spend cap, check the card on file, and give at least two people admin access on both platforms and Merchant Center, with two-step verification on devices they’ll have over the holiday.

Several Google Ads features that add promotions or pick landing pages are on by default, so go through them before your own promotion goes live.

I wouldn’t switch all of this off on principle. Decide on each one during the holidays and note what you changed so you can revisit it in January.

Your brand campaign should be fully funded through Cyber Monday, and even into December. Keep an eye on auction insights daily to see which competitors are bidding on your brand. I know I’m stating the obvious, but this is definitely not the time of the year to let a competitor steal a brand sale. Be defensive, buy your brand terms, and keep that impression share % high. Keeping brand in its own campaign, which I’ve argued for before, makes a “Limited By Budget” status obvious the morning it happens.

On one premium brand we work with, several competitors were bidding on the brand name, and we’ve consistently managed brand spend throughout the year, but during holiday shopping times, we max out impression share %.

Once the checks are done, the hardest part of Black Friday advertising is leaving the account alone and letting it run. Of course, make sure there is someone keeping an eye on it from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday and have a plan in place for what can change. Does pacing increase at all? If so, what % increase is the cap? Should any creative be swapped out? Messaging?

We keep that checklist pretty short: budgets on campaigns that are hitting target and fixes for tracking or disapprovals, and everything else waits until Dec. 1.

Keep a running list throughout the week of anything you couldn’t fix, whether that’s prospecting you never built, creative you didn’t get to test, or the budget you wish you’d started with in early November. It’s the most useful thing you’ll have when you start planning next year’s holiday season, and it’s a lot easier to write down this week than to piece together in January, or even next year.

Check that budgets have ramped, that tracking records the right value on a real promo order, that billing won’t stop your ads, and that your offer matches across site, feed, and ads. Campaigns and creative should already be built, so the week is for checks and fixes.

Enough that your best campaigns aren’t capped on Black Friday or Cyber Monday, based on your own past results rather than a round number. With Cyber Monday on November 30, set Google budgets before the weekend, since a budget raised on the last day of the month only gets one day of room.

For this year, mostly yes. In our accounts, upper-funnel spend takes roughly six to eight weeks to show up in revenue, so prospecting launched now is bought at peak prices and mostly pays out in January. Keep what you have running and plan next year’s build for September.

No. Results from BFCM week don’t carry over well to the rest of the year, and an untested concept is an expensive bet at peak prices. Put the offer on proven creative and test in October.

Yes. If competitors bid on your brand and you don’t, you can lose those sales to them. Keep brand in its own campaign with enough budget and check auction insights daily through Cyber Week.

#7270. Last of the old school buyers, Publicis Media vet John Muszynski prepares to retire

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

He’s equally comfortable at the negotiating table or on skates in an ice rink.

He doesn’t do it himself but he knows principal media is part of the business.

He’s said to have once humbled the CEO of a major cable network group by holding back $200 million of his clients’ media spend when that CEO tried to bully him into big price increases.

He’s the longest-serving head of investment in media. And now, John Muszynski, legendary media investment executive with Publicis Media, plans to retire.

After 45 years at one holding company and negotiating nearly as many upfronts over that span, the chairman of Publicis Media Exchange (PMX) U.S., is stepping down from a full-time role this year, although he plans to continue to consult with the holdco.

Chicago-based Muszynski, who oversees decision-making on what Publicis estimates to be 40% of the U.S. video marketplace inventory, is arguably the last of the old-school heads of investment that have seen the upfronts morph into the byzantine bazaar it is today.

“For nearly five decades, I’ve had a front row seat to the industry’s transformation,” Muszynski told Digiday. “It’s gone from three networks to always-on content spanning the entire digital ecosystem. It’s been fascinating to be a part of it all.”

The avid ice hockey fan, hunter and fisherman (when he’s not negotiating) got his start in 1981 as a planner for Leo Burnett’s burgeoning media unit, handling longtime Publicis clients including Kimberly-Clark, McDonald’s and Kellogg’s. That unit eventually became standalone media agency Starcom, for which he rose to CEO of Starcom USA from 2005-2009. He then helped to build Spark Foundry from a 65-person boutique into a 3,000-person media agency.

In 2016, Publicis formed Publicis Media Exchange, which harnessed the collective buying clout of what was then Starcom, Mediavest, Spark, Zenith, Optimedia and Blue 449 media agencies. He was the lead negotiator when that formed, and became chairman of the group in 2022.

The execs who sat across from him at the negotiating table said they always felt they got a fair shake — in part because Muszynski always came prepared, was knowledgable and true to his word.

“John has been a tremendous influence on generations of marketers, agency team members and publishers,” said Mark Marshall, chairman of global advertising and partnerships at NBCUniversal. “He has always put his clients’ objectives at the forefront and pushed all of us to deliver for those clients. He is the epitome of ‘a handshake is his word’.”

Rita Ferro, president, global advertising, disney, was even more personal in her assessment of working with Muszynski. “John is a legend in this business and from the moment we met, he became a trusted partner and more importantly a dear friend,” she said.

Sean Moran, COO at Evergreen Trading agency, who negotiated with Muszynski during his 24 years as an ad sales exec with Viacom until 2020, thinks of Muszynski as a contemporary of the old-school buyers of the TV business, from Grey Advertising’s Jon Mandel to UM’s Donna Wolfe, and from Omnicom’s John Swift to GroupM’s Rino Scanzoni.

“When I was running MTV and we had a big upfront event, and had to get people there, if I could get John Muszynski to fly in and come to my event, that was a huge win,” said Moran. ”He represented so much gravitas. Obviously he controlled a lot of budgets, but it was also because he was so smart and yet had such empathy for good people. You couldn’t bullshit him. He was a good Midwestern guy who could talk about a great deal over over a steak, but he did his homework and knew his numbers.”

Moran said Muszynski often set the marketplace as “the main controller” of the upfronts. “One of his negotiating tactics was, ‘Yeah, I haven’t seen everything, but boy, it looks down’,” said Moran. “If he respected your inventory, you could do a deal with him fairly quickly and cut through the chaff. He was known to pull that with one or two people that were at the front of the line, and protect his clients. He would therefore set the marketplace for himself. It was very smart.”

Although Muszynski will retire from his full-time position at PMX, he will stay on to consult through 2027, working with Joel Lunenfeld who leads PMX globally and Mark Griffin, who oversees all investment in the U.S. as chief investment officer.

The platform rolled out various updates for the format, including the much-requested option to make changes to Stories after posting.

Instagram has rolled out a range of updates for Stories, including a much-requested editing option, which will enable users to update their posts after publishing.

As shown in this image, Instagram users will now be able to edit published Stories for up to 15 minutes after posting. Which isn't a huge window of time, but it should be enough to catch and correct any typos or mistakes.

It’s a significant update, which will be particularly beneficial for social media managers, enabling them to revise their content instead of having to start over again.

Instagram has also made it easier to select and post multiple images in Stories and added more display options.

The updates will provide more ways for users to share their experiences in Stories during the upcoming holiday season, while as noted, they'll also help marketers use Stories to promote their holiday offers.

On another front, Instagram added the capacity to search saved items in the iOS version of the app.

As shown in these images, posted by app researcher Radu Oncescu, Instagram users can now search within their saved items. It’s a minor functional addition, but it could be a big help in finding previously saved posts.

#7266. Google Says Back Button Hijacking Policy Covers Social Visits via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Google says the back button hijacking policy applies to visits from social media and other channels, and that sites can keep using ad platform code.

Google’s back button hijacking policy applies whenever the hijacking happens in a browser, including on visits from social media rather than Google Search, according to an FAQ Google added to its spam policies today.

Ad platform code is still allowed, the FAQ says, and Google acts only on pages that show the hijacking.

Google’s Search Central changelog says the FAQ answers common questions it has received about the policy. I covered the policy when Google announced it in April, with enforcement set to start June 15.

One FAQ question asks whether the back button hijacking policy covers people who arrive from a non-Search channel, such as social media, and then can’t get back to where they came from. Google wrote:

“If back button hijacking happens when a user is browsing within a browser, then the policy applies.”

A separate answer says “Discover is a part of Google Search and our spam policies apply to Discover as well.” That answer covers Google’s spam policies in general, not only this one.

For a website that opens an external app, which then keeps the user from getting back to the site, the FAQ says “app navigation and ‘open in app’ behaviors are outside the scope of the back button hijacking policy.”

Google’s FAQ shows how the policy applies to visits in a browser and where external app navigation falls outside its scope.

Google’s April announcement said some back button hijacking “may originate from the site’s included libraries or advertising platform,” and asked sites to remove or turn off the code behind it.

The FAQ asks whether Google is preventing sites from importing code hosted by advertising platforms. Google wrote:

“No, site owners can continue to work with advertising platforms and import code that they host. We only take action on pages that exhibit back button hijacking behavior.”

A back button test that starts from a Google results page doesn’t cover every visit the hijacking policy applies to. Test pages that carry ad code by arriving from a social media link and pressing back, and repeat it from Discover when one of your pages shows up there.

Google’s answer on ad code lets you keep your ad partners. The thing to remove is the code or setting on a page that interferes with the back button, wherever it comes from.

Google’s FAQ also says users can report back button hijacking through its spam report form. Those reports go toward improving Google’s spam detection systems, which gives people who hit hijacking on a social or Discover visit a way to flag a site.

#7264. LinkedIn study explores B2B buying decisions

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The research highlights the importance of relational factors, such as testimonials and peer validation, when it comes to influencing client purchases.

LinkedIn has published new research which examines what drives B2B buying decisions, and provides guidance on how brands can ensure that their products are as appealing as possible to prospective clients.

The study, conducted in conjunction with WARC and Lions Advisory, analyzes the factors that go into creating "buyability." The authors examined 700 B2B case studies in order to discover the crucial factors that influence purchase decisions across these examples.

The findings show that many of the key factors that drive decision-making are relational, as opposed to being grounded in product functionality.

As explained by Mimi Turner, global head of thought leadership strategy at LinkedIn’s B2B Institute: “Confidence in product capability is still very important. But once baseline requirements are met, the top priority is no longer marginal product superiority or price. It becomes whether the decision can be successfully defended even if outcomes go wrong.”

In order to test this, the study measured each of the 700 campaigns against various criteria related to buying signals.

The researchers then segmented the campaigns into "high buyability" campaigns, which were those that included three or more of these signals, and "low buyability" initiatives, which included zero, one or two signals.

The results shoed that high buyability campaigns — meaning those with more focus on testimonials, peer validation and measures of industry leadership — significantly outperformed low buyability campaigns across commercial and brand measures.

“Evaluated against the WARC B2B Effectiveness Ladder, High Buyability campaigns were also 1.7x more likely to be classified as ‘Strategic Assets,’ the highest rung of effectiveness, reserved for initiatives that drive sustained commercial growth,” Turner said.

The data also found that customer-centric insights were present in 83% of high buyability campaigns, which were also four times more likely to feature customer testimonials.

In other words, including more elements that reinforce buying decisions through relatable examples and external validation can have a major impact on reassuring buyers and securing more deals.

LinkedIn further tested these concepts in a campaign for ServiceNow, which specifically focused on these buyability elements.

“The results included a 10x increase in consideration, a 13x increase in unaided brand awareness over three years, and subscription revenue up by 23% over the same period,” Turner said.

Turner said these findings indicate that recommendations, relationships and relatable buying situations can have a significant influence on campaign outcomes.

These notes could help B2B marketers improve the resonance of their campaigns.

#7261. I Blind-Tested 3 Gemini Models On Real SEO Questions – Neon Won 5 Of 6 via @sejournal, @marie_haynes

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Is the newest AI model actually better, or do we just assume it is? My blind test of three Gemini models gave a clear answer.

Over the last few months, I have been quietly building something I call Marie’s Brain – a private AI co-pilot grounded in my hand-curated Open Knowledge Format (OKF) library of Search and AI research.

Recently, I switched the tool over to Google’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. After using it for a while, though, I had a nagging feeling: Is Hydrogen actually producing better answers than Gemini 3.8 Flash, or am I just assuming newer means better?

Instead of guessing, I decided to run a real blind taste test – and threw Gemini 4 Neon into the mix too.

You can actually try the exact same six-question blind test yourself here (columns A, B, and C are shuffled on every question, and there is a button at the top to reveal how I voted and the real token costs).

The blind 3-way taste test interface: columns A, B, and C are shuffled on every SEO question, complete with clickable OKF concept pills. Try voting blind yourself here. Image Credit: Marie Haynes

Before I even finished reading the first round of blind outputs, one thing jumped out immediately: The answers were way too long.

My Brain had been defaulting to Detailed mode with no word ceiling. When we checked the API logs, we discovered something wild: Gemini 4 Hydrogen was going into an over-eager research loop, reading an average of 21 OKF files per question, taking 68 seconds, writing 1,600-word essays, and costing $0.44 per prompt – actually more expensive per turn than Gemini 4 Neon!

On top of that, some answers were dropping internal Google engineering jargon (like MAGIT and FastSearch) that a busy business owner does not need to wade through just to figure out why their clicks dropped.

So before doing my real blind vote, I made three quick upgrades to how Marie’s Brain works:

Then we re-ran the exact same six real-world SEO and AI Search questions – covering AI Overviews and traffic drops, whether to delete or rewrite informational posts, Main Content on commercial buyer’s guides, pruning thin location pages, agent readiness and /llms.txt, and a realistic five-hour-a-week plan that skips GEO distractions – across Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 4 Hydrogen, and Gemini 4 Neon.

With the model names hidden and the columns randomized, I read all 18 answers and picked a winner on every prompt.

When I hit reveal, the result wasn’t even close:

What stood out to me about Neon wasn’t that it had more facts – all three models pulled from the exact same OKF files. It was how it communicated. Neon’s answers felt more like a smart human thinking through a problem rather than a predictable AI response. I genuinely enjoyed reading them, and I immediately understood what they were trying to get across.

My revealed blind test results (5/6 for Gemini 4 Neon), real Gemini API token usage, and pace-adjusted monthly cost estimates per user. Image Credit: Marie Haynes

Of course, better answers only matter if the economics make sense. Here are the real numbers from our live Concise-mode runs (using real Gemini API usageMetadata, including thinking tokens, at conservative uncached list rates):

Note on Neon’s speed: That 70.8s average was skewed by one single 3.5-minute API queue spike during testing; typical Neon replies ran 18 to 40 seconds (with text streaming on screen as it writes).

At first glance, $191 vs. $93 per 1,000 prompts sounds like a big jump (about 10 cents extra per prompt). But when I mapped that against realistic full-month usage paces extrapolated from my early active users, here is what the extra cost per user looks like:

And those are conservative uncached estimates. Because every turn references the same ~55,000-token OKF Master Index, Gemini 4 Neon’s implicit context caching discounts repeated input tokens across multi-turn chats, bringing real-world bills noticeably lower.

#7259. Correcting the TV ad market’s imperfect shift to streaming

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Evan Rutchik, president and Chief Strategy Officer, Viamedia.ai

The TV ad industry’s shift from linear to streaming is real, but the financial truth underlying that shift may not align with many people’s perception of the transition. That’s because the movement of ad budgets from linear to streaming has hardly been evenly paced.

Streaming’s share of ad revenue is indeed growing at major media companies, including The Walt Disney Company, Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. But their earnings tell a different story: Linear revenue is falling faster than streaming revenue is rising. The shift is happening, but it’s not benefiting content owners as expected.

The core problem is a supply-demand imbalance. Streaming ad revenue is growing through increased volume, not higher prices. New inventory floods in, making cheap inventory abundant. As major subscription services continue to promote free ad-supported streaming tiers, the buyers’ market will only continue.

The solution is to grow demand, not increase prices. Fortunately, the ad dollars needed to support the streaming market already exist, sitting in local and midmarket budgets that haven’t been able to buy national CTV efficiently. The opportunity is to bring these advertisers into the broader video and streaming market, then develop ways to keep them investing.

Correcting the imbalance requires creating new demand, then ensuring that content quality and product performance are strong enough to eventually shift pricing dynamics.

When it comes to growth, the glut of cheap national SVOD supply may be a problem for programmers, but it’s an opportunity for local and midmarket advertisers. If the current streaming market is largely aimed at Fortune 500 companies, the industry has to consider the thousands of smaller advertisers that make steady annual investments in local linear buys. Taken collectively, these advertisers represent billions of dollars in ad budgets.

Because these advertisers have smaller budgets, many haven’t tried streaming. It is more cost-efficient for them to execute local and spot buys on linear than to invest in targeted or national streaming campaigns. These advertisers are still seeing real success reaching millions of linear viewers, so they understand the power of TV. They just need an entry point for CTV. Solving this issue would allow demand to flow steadily into the market.

Once that demand enters the market, additional steps must happen. CPMs fall when inventory is sold as undifferentiated tonnage. With platforms like Disney+ and Netflix exploring free ad-supported tiers, even more low-cost supply will enter the market. But cheap supply that doesn’t perform isn’t worth an advertiser’s investment. If that inventory doesn’t deliver results for advertisers outside the Fortune 500, those advertisers will invest their budgets elsewhere, creating another demand imbalance.

The answer lies in household addressability. While this is available on some streaming platforms, it’s still largely absent from the overall TV market, including linear. Household-level addressability turns cheap impressions into targeted impressions worth buying, even within highly premium inventory. The more information brands have about who will see their ads and whether those ads are likely to resonate with the viewer, the more they are likely to pay.

It is no secret that streaming is the future of TV, and shifting revenue numbers reflect that. To build a sustainable future for media companies and advertisers, the entire ecosystem must first provide ease of access and then addressability.

Making streaming easier to buy at scale would help solve the demand problem. Once more advertisers are in the market, addressability creates greater competition for impressions, solving the pricing imbalance.

This future is out there, provided the industry takes a few steps in the right direction.

Holiday marketing is changing: CTV/streaming and TV ads are gaining traction in 2026.

#7256. Check Who’s Posting Before You Trust Reddit On AEO Tools via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

An analysis of subreddits flagged most users weighing in on AEO tools as likely promoters. Among the rest, accuracy was the top feature complaint.

Graphite flagged 55% of the users who gave an opinion of an AEO tool across 54 subreddits this year as likely working for or promoting a marketing software product.

Among the users it didn’t flag, the accuracy of visibility scores drew more unfavorable opinions than any other product feature.

The growth agency picked subreddits where AEO comes up regularly and found 5,990 posts and 25,392 comments from January through September that mention a tool. OpenAI language models labeled the mentions, the opinions and the likely promoters.

The agency helps companies with AEO and SEO and says it doesn’t sell AEO tools or accept payment to be mentioned. Its CEO, Ethan Smith, is an investor in Peec AI, one of three tools tied for the highest score in the analysis.

Graphite flagged 1,298 of the 2,365 Reddit users who gave an opinion of an AEO tool or a marketing platform’s AEO features.

A user was flagged when the agency’s model put the chance at 50% or more that their posts promoted a marketing product they build, own, work for, sell or partner with. That includes SEO, AEO, sales and web analytics tools. An agency’s description of its own client work did not constitute promotion.

To test the model, the company manually inspected 43 of the users it had flagged. Ultimately, 12% of them disclosed being promoters, while 62% were found to have promoted a product but failed to identify themselves as such; the remaining ones were judged non-promoters. The write-up also says that some of the models’ labeling decisions could be incorrect.

Four types of likely promoter Reddit accounts were identified. Each type exhibited a pattern across several posts or comments.

One account was used to recommend the same lesser-known tracking service on eight posts and comments. In January this user claimed that they switched from a competitor, and 11 days later they commented about possibly purchasing the product.

Another account made reference to a little-known product in four comments with well-known tracking services over the course of eight days.

A third account posted three separate times for the same product within 12 minutes.

Over six weeks, 38 accounts recommended the same product in 52 comments, each using the phrase “from what I’ve read” in its recommendation. That phrase appears with any other tool no more than twice.

Of the opinions regarding the accuracy of AEO tools from users who weren’t flagged, 143 were negative while 27 had positive views. No other feature elicited as many negative opinions. These users provided opinions on 44 tools, for a total of 1,557 opinions.

Graphite’s chart compares praise and criticism across features after excluding opinions from users it flagged as likely promoters.

According to the write-up, users frequently view visibility scores as estimates due to variation in AI answers among different runs, locations and users. Several have advised fellow users to “treat them as trend, not truth” and to verify the information through manual review.

The citation data, or the citations used by AI systems as source material for their answers, was generally viewed positively by users. Price received more user opinions than any other attribute and most of those opinions were negative, at 182 negative versus 98 positive.

The agency also evaluated the 11 tools which generated sufficient opinions using a 0-100 point scale; a score of 50 represented neutral. Each of the 11 tools scored between 54 and 66 points. The authors also said the ranges around many of the tools’ scores overlapped and therefore, the differences in scores could lack statistical significance.

Graphite’s count puts a number on how many Reddit users weighing in on AEO tools may be promoting marketing software. Before a tool recommended on Reddit goes on your shortlist, check the account’s history for repeat plugs and a story that changes from post to post.

Graphite’s tool scores reflect opinions from January through September, and the company says their order could change as more opinions come in. Complaints about the accuracy of visibility scores give you something to test before renewing. Run a sample of your tracked prompts by hand and compare the results with the tool’s numbers.

#7253. Meta launches shopping platform in Brazil

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Achados combines product listings from across the company’s apps into a unified display.

Meta has launched yet another experimental app, with the company’s new shopping-focused platform, called Achados, now available to users in Brazil.

Achados is a marketplace app that combines product listings from across Meta’s other platforms into a single, unified display of what’s available for purchase.

As per the app’s description in the Google Play store: “One feed for what people near you are selling: listings from Marketplace, posts from Facebook Groups, and items sellers have shared from Instagram, including listings you won’t find in a Marketplace search.”

As shown in the third image above, the app also includes a price comparison element, which shows how each listing matches up against similar products available in Meta’s apps.

Achados also enables potential buyers to view seller profiles on Facebook and IG, and includes customer reviews and sales histories.

According to reporting from El Fondo, Achados launched in Brazil on Tuesday, and is only available on Android at this stage.

Meta has been on an app spree of late, with the company launching six new apps this year alone, all focused on different elements.

Meta is also reportedly working on a prediction markets app, as another way to potentially expand its suite of tools.

Meta has always experimented with new apps, and most of them end up seeing limited engagement, with Meta mainly using them as a learning experience for features in its main app instead.

But the evolution of generative AI has enabled Meta to pump out app experiments more quickly, which lets the company try out more things and capitalize on common behaviors and opportunities as identified by its internal developers.

In this context, the focus on selling is noteworthy. Achados essentially aims to build on Meta’s broader shopping potential by merging all of the various product listings across its apps into a single feed.

That could provide a range of expanded promotional opportunities, while also potentially driving more shopping behavior in Meta’s other apps.

Also worth noting: Meta recently expanded its Creator Fast Track program to creators in Brazil. The combined announcements could suggest that Meta is looking to capitalize on rising opportunities in the country.

#7250. OpenAI rewrites ChatGPT Business Hub terms after legal language raises concerns

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

OpenAI has revised the terms for its new ChatGPT Business Hub days after its launch. The change came after Digiday reported that lawyers viewed the original language as potentially limiting businesses’ ability to bring certain legal claims against the company.

Launched last week, the Business Hub gives businesses that verify their accounts direct data on how their websites appear in ChatGPT, including mentions, profile views, clicks and discovery topics. For publishers, it’s a first-party view of activity they’ve largely had to estimate.

Before the revision, Section 10 of OpenAI’s terms of service for businesses using ChatGPT appeared to require those businesses to give up certain legal claims against OpenAI, lawyers told Digiday. They said the language could apply to claims involving content published on their websites, before they signed up.

The terms included a mandatory arbitration provision and class-action waiver, potentially requiring businesses to resolve disputes individually and outside of court, Chapell said. The provision was broadly worded to cover certain claims that arose before the agreement was accepted, he explained.

Businesses had 30 days to opt out of arbitration, but if they did not, they could have faced limits on their ability to obtain evidence, pursue appeals and establish legal precedent through public court proceedings, Chapell added.

This could’ve put a chokehold on publishers that are in the midst of figuring out how to protect and monetize their content in the AI era, potentially limiting their ability to bring copyright infringement claims against OpenAI down the road.

Hours after Digiday first contacted OpenAI on Nov. 18, the terms were revised. They now include a waiver of businesses’ rights to seek a court order preventing OpenAI from using certain customer data, according to an IP and tech lawyer, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

“There are still some restrictions here but they don’t leave a customer completely without recourse. A customer could still, even if not entirely practical, sue for monetary damages,” they said.

When approached for comment, an OpenAI spokesperson said the previous version of the terms “were not intended to cover this scenario,” and confirmed it updated the terms on Nov. 18.

“We continually evaluate the language in our Terms to make sure they are as clear as possible,” the spokesperson added in a statement. “The updated terms replace the separate ‘covered claims’ provision with language in Section 5.2 that ties the release to claims arising from a business’s Business Agent, including the use of customer data with that agent.”

One industry exec, who requested anonymity, told Digiday they advised publishers’ legal teams to be cautious around some of the potential implications of OpenAI’s terms for businesses, after they were originally published on Nov. 10.

Although the terms have been revised, several lawyers who spoke to Digiday said the original version was likely deliberate.

“This is certainly not an oversight because they put these terms out there,” said Gary Kibel, partner at law firm Davis+ Gilbert, which advises media and advertising clients. “It was incredibly intentional, and they were seeking to use this opportunity to get a release and wavier for any of these claims. It seems to be quite aggressive to do that.”

Kibel said the revised terms still require businesses to waive certain legal claims related to their use of ChatGPT Business Hub and its AI Business Agents (essentially a business-specific chatbot), but no longer extend that waiver to unrelated legal disputes with OpenAI.

OpenAI’s changes come just weeks after Meta faced major backlash from publishers over its new commercial terms, which would have allowed the company to scrape the websites of Meta Business account users. The proposed changes spurred a global, coordinated pushback from publishers, trade bodies, and government officials and regulators. In response, Meta announced it would pause the rollout until it has had time to explain the changes to key stakeholders and partners.

OpenAI’s terms revision also follows tensions between publishers and AI companies over the use of published content. Documents unsealed in The New York Times’ lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft two months ago revealed tech giants were treating published content as free fuel for AI products that threatened their very existence.

Whatever prompted the revision, it may do little to ease publishers’ broader concerns about how AI companies use their content, and the terms attached to new tools built around that content.

#7248. TikTok adds new AI transparency and parental controls

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The platform announced a range of updates at its third Safety and Innovation Summit, including new ways to protect creators and teens.

TikTok announced a range of updates at its third Safety and Innovation Summit last week, including a new tool that helps users identify artificial intelligence-generated content, a likeness detection feature to protect creator IP and new tools and resources for parents and schools.

First, TikTok announced a new AI transparency tool that will enable users to check if an image or video has been created using its AI tools.

As explained by TikTok: “People can upload an image or video to see whether it was generated or edited with TikTok’s AI creation features, even if they don’t have a TikTok account.”

The process will check the image or video for signs of TikTok’s digital watermarking on AI-generated content, providing another means to verify content in the app. That could also help to stop the spread of misinformation and harmful content.

TikTok said the tool is now available via its Transparency Center.

TikTok also announced a likeness detection tool that enables creators to verify their likeness, which will then facilitate image cross-matching against incoming uploads.

TikTok said creators will verify their ID with a trusted third-party partner, which will empower the system to detect and raise awareness of content that includes their image.

“They can report content directly to our safety teams,” the company said. “Content that violates our community guidelines against harmful, misleading or nonconsensual depiction of private individuals will be removed.”

The tool is now available to eligible creators and public figures.

TikTok also announced updates to its Family Pairing process, in order to give parents more visibility into how their teens are using the app and who they’re connecting with.

TikTok's updated Family Pairing also now includes more data on what kids are posting, as well as a new element that will enable parents to see what their kids are being shown in the app.

As explained by TikTok: “Parents can watch a sample of content from verified creators their teen follows, providing a snapshot of the communities and topic areas shaping their experience. More than 80% of parents of teens that we spoke to told us they want this kind of feature.”

TikTok also made its screen time element more prominent to help ensure that parents are aware of how much time their kids are spending in the app, and when in the day they’re active.

TikTok said it’s also working with leading experts to build a new alert for parents, which will let them know if their teen makes repeated searches for known terms related to self-harm.

“This notification will let them know that their teen may have tried to find potentially harmful content and provide thoughtful, expert-backed guidance on how to check in and start a conversation,” TikTok said.

Finally, TikTok launched a new Educator's Guide, which will provide teachers with additional resources to help advise teens on mindful social media usage behaviors.

These additional AI insight tools and the new parental experience controls should offer more ways for people to understand what’s happening in the app.

That could also provide more assurance for parents. And with more regions considering teen social media bans, additional understanding could also help TikTok reduce negative sentiment around the app.

#7247. How SharkNinja is doubling down on its creator strategy

The home appliance brand introduced two new creator programs, SharkNinja First Fans and SharkNinja Storytellers, to tap into the quickly growing influencer economy.

SharkNinja CEO Mark Barrocas in 2008 told a retailer that his plan was to build the company “one five-star review at a time.” In Barrocas’ retelling, the retailer’s executives dismissed the idea as foolish because they couldn’t imagine who would write a review of the brand’s products. That was before the rise of influencers.

Over the ensuing 28 years, SharkNinja has become a multibillion-dollar global company, which built its brand through a social-forward, ultra-connected strategy that includes partnerships with celebrities including David Beckham, Courteney Cox and Alix Earle, alongside a host of influencers.

SharkNinja is doubling down on that strategy with two new programs designed to give storytellers, both inside and outside of the company, access and opportunities to develop and create even more content.

The programs, SharkNinja First Fans, for company employees, and SharkNinja Storytellers, for general consumers and creators, are designed to help the company continue to grow and manage its expanding list of creators and partners.

“We felt we were underserving this community by not creating a space where we could have more scaled one-to-ones with them, bring them further into the fold in terms of our product board maps, and incentivize participation,” said Michelle Crossan-Matos, chief brand and experience officer at SharkNinja.

Over 200,000 posts about SharkNinja’s varied household products, which include blenders, vacuums and ice-cream makers, have been made this year, garnering more than 19 billion impressions, according to the company. Last year, it recorded more than $6.4 billion in sales.

The secret sauce is the company’s practice of fostering, nurturing and actively supporting those who want to create content around SharkNinja’s products, according to Crossan-Matos.

“We bring creators all the way upstream with our products, and we’re having them react to and test and make content with some of our products before we go to market. It’s always been core for our strategy,” said Crossan-Matos.

The new programs use leaderboards and rewards to ensure the content keeps coming. For outside creators, the rewards, which can include commissions and perks, are tied to growth and activity. The most active creators will get exclusive first looks at upcoming products and even get a voice in shaping them. The company has created tutorials and other materials, including an artificial intelligence-powered app, to help the internal creators develop compelling narratives.

Though not exactly commonplace, employer-supported creator programs are not unheard of either. Starbucks has its Green Apron Creators, IBM has a Buzz Squad, Gap opened up its creator ecosystem to employees, and Dell has compensated its employees for sharing content on their own channels. The scope of SharkNinja’s creator efforts are notable.

“I don't know if anybody is doing it the exact way that we are,” Crossan-Matos said. “I think to have both [consumer and employee programs] launch as quickly as we did and at this scale … Our appetite is to drive this globally.”

The company can support these programs on a global scale because of its broad product base, Crossan-Matos said. SharkNinja creates products across 41 consumer categories and launches an average of 25 new products every year.

“We're very lucky to have so many products for so many different types of communities globally,” Crossan-Matos said. “Creators just fit so seamlessly into our co-creation and our storytelling. We think [these initiatives] are going to propel more people to tell their own stories in a way that is even more relatable because they're everyday people.”

Keeping an eye on metrics will be key to measuring program success.

“We’ll be looking at content performance, just like we do with everything. We will be looking for what posts are going viral, what things are gaining traction,” Crossan-Matos said. “We expect really high numbers as we expand.”

#7246. YouTube adds co-view counts to CTV metrics

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The platform will now CTV view counts based on television industry standards, and apply those new view counts across formats moving forward.

YouTube will now report higher viewer counts on CTV, with the addition of co-views to its CTV stats. YouTube said that the expanded numbers will provide a more accurate reflection of total viewer numbers.

As per YouTube, CTV viewing has become a major part of the YouTube experience, with over a billion hours of YouTube content now being watched on TV sets every day. But videos watched via CTV are often viewed by several people sitting in front of a TV set together, and as such, YouTube’s current CTV view count metric approach is too limited, because it only shows a single viewer per CTV session. That’s why the company is updating how it counts CTV views.

The solution, however, is based on estimates, because YouTube can’t track actual CTV viewer counts.

YouTube announced the addition of co-views in May, when Rene Ritchie, the platform’s head of editorial, gave an overview of the logic behind how YouTube will calculate co-views.

At the time, Ritchie said that YouTube would add additional viewers to CTV views “based on factors like demographics, video genre, even time of day.”

In its most recent announcement, Ritchie provided more clarity, saying that co-views would provide a more complete picture, “aligning with TV industry standards, including how traditional broadcast and streaming networks estimate the total number of people exposed to content.”

So how does the TV industry estimate TV viewers?

Audience analytics company Nielsen uses a people meter with families who take part in its research panel, which sees different family members manually reporting their viewing behaviors via response buttons when they're watching. The rise of VOD services with individual log-ins has expanded the pool of information on this front, and based on these sources, YouTube appears to be using an industry-standard estimation measure to suggest total CTV viewers of each video, which will then be reflected in its view counts.

Which won’t be exact, of course, but it could be more accurate than the current system.

Ritchie added that historical view counts won't be changed, and that co-views will only be applied to new TV views, including new views of old videos.

Ritchie also said that co-views won't impact ad revenue or YPP thresholds, while, creator earnings, AdSense payouts and YouTube partner program eligibility will still be based on qualified views and watch hours.

Though the change will impact watch time metrics.

As per Ritchie “While co-views also don't impact metrics like thumbnail impressions, click-through rates and average view duration, watch time will be consistent with the updated public view counts to reflect the co-view audience watching together.”

In other words, watch time calculations will rise based on the assumption that more people are watching at certain times. So if YouTube estimated that three people were watching a video, for example, the watch time count for that video would then be tripled for that session.

The change will see many YouTube videos get higher view counts and watch time results, so if there’s a sudden spike in these metrics, this is likely why.

YouTube’s co-view update is being rolled out to all channels.

The Staff GTM Systems Engineer at LiveKit is the technical owner and architect of the systems that power our go-to-market engine. #7243. Bumble cozies up to Alix Earle in attempt to convert Gen Zers

The influencer, who has previously stated her dislike of dating apps, appears in a two-minute video alongside Pete Davidson to encourage Gen Z users to give the platform a try.

Bumble is looking to appeal to Gen Z users as the demographic continues to ditch apps for real-life alternatives. User retention continues to be a problem for the dating app, which saw the total number of paying users decline from 2.5 million in Q2 2025 to 2.1 million in Q2 2026, according to an earnings statement.

The casting choices for the campaign are interesting ones as Earle has routinely rejected dating apps and Davidson is known for his string of ill-fated relationships with high-profile individuals, including a short-lived engagement to pop star Ariana Grande.

The video is self-aware regarding the history of its stars. For example, when Davidson plays an inconsiderate first date, Earle asks what Davidson does for work. He responds "Nothing much. I just kind of talk to camera.” Earle responds that she does something similar, to which Davidson replies, “yeah, but when I do it, it’s different,” a reference to controversial comments the comedian made regarding large influencer salaries and the amount of work involved.

Earle’s character is similarly aware of her past with dating apps. When confronted with the fact that she has publicly stated she hates dating apps, she responds: “I have said that publicly at least five different times on three different platforms. But sometimes I can be a little dramatic.”

Over the course of the sexual innuendo-laden spot, Earle convinces her fellow Gen Zers to try Bumble, showing off features such as searching for specific people. The women are impressed by the quality of men they find on the site, with one participant being impressed they all have bedframes.

The campaign was created in partnership with OBB Bolded and is supported by Bumble data that found 81% of singles between the ages of 18 and 25 are most interested in a relationship that adds value to the life they’re building.

Bumble has worked to attract more users to its app in recent months, including allowing anyone in a match to send the first message, a deviation away from the previous model where women had to send the first message, which was once a selling point for the brand. It also expanded the response window from 24 to 72 hours and introduced handles, a tool that allows verified users to more easily find one another on the app.

This isn’t the first time Bumble has turned to influencer marketing. In June, the app launched “Bee Line,” a talk show hosted by comedian and influencer Jake Shane that tackles dating anxiety.

#7241. Instagram chief shares Muse tips for social media managers

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Adam Mosseri told Marina Mogilko, aka Silicon Valley Girl, that the artificial intelligence agent can help with ideation and trend discovery.

As Meta continues to expand access to its Muse artificial intelligence agents, which were made available to Australian users last week, social media managers may be wondering how they can use the tool within their process.

Instagram creator Marina Mogilko, who goes by the handle “Silicon Valley Girl,” recently interviewed Instagram Chief Adam Mosseri to get his insights on how creators and social media managers can use Meta’s AI agent to grow Instagram reach.

Mosseri said that Muse is good for ideation and coming up with resonant content concepts.

As per Mosseri: “If you’re trying to come up with more ideas, telling [Muse] what your goal is, then asking it for 10, 20, 30, 50 ideas, telling Muse which ones you like and which you don’t and iterating, it’s a great way just to get, sometimes, the creative juices going.”

Mosseri added that Muse can be helpful for evaluating content performance, and can assess what’s worked and what hasn’t in posts. He said the AI agent can also help categorize content.

Finally, Mosseri said Muse can be helpful for understanding trends.

“So for your audience, or for your industry, what are the trends that are happening right now on social media, not even just on Instagram,”Mosseri said. “Because that might surface conversations that you might want to jump in, for instance.”

Mogilko also asked Mosseri about Muse’s capacity to analyze followers, and provide assessment on the most influential followers in any sector. Mosseri said that Muse can provide a level of assessment of a profile’s audience, but Instagram is working on making this more valuable and effective.

Also interesting: Last month, Meta ran an ad for Muse which promoted the fact that the agent can alert Instagram users to people who have unfollowed them. Though as reported by Business Insider, it quickly took down the promotion after realizing that it goes against Instagram’s ethos.

Wired also reported that some people have been using Muse to unfollow accounts that don’t follow them back.

The latter two use cases are probably not what Meta wants to promote, but they do provide additional considerations for how the agent could be used to assist in automating some aspects of digital marketing.

#7240. Why more brands are paying creators to make their ads

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

This article is part of an ongoing series detailing the most important information readers need to know about the ad industry’s most complex topics. More from the series →

Brands paying influencers to make campaign creative have become key drivers of investment in the booming creator economy. Creative agencies might want to take note.

“You get the authentic, scroll-stopping content that people want to engage each with. But you also get the reach,” said Katy Ball, head of social at M&C Saatchi Sport & Entertainment.

As spending on paid social channels — and video in particular — continues to rise, demand for creative assets to appear in those ad slots is increasing.

The number of assets attached to individual campaigns has risen 30% in the last five years, according to a CreativeX study of 115,990 ad campaigns, representing $11 billion in ad spend. Per the study, just five assets receive 88% of media investment in an average campaign.

The need for more campaign assets is fueling the growth of asset-led spending, the fastest growing segment of the creator economy, according to a report published this week by research consultancy Madison & Wall.

Currently, 12% of the $112 billion spent on creators globally goes towards creators producing ads on behalf of brands, per the study. That’s expected to rise 16% every year through 2030.

The days when brands principally paid creators to rent their following are rapidly disappearing. Influencers are now media partners, ambassadors and increasingly, cogs in the creative production supply chain. And brands see creator-made ads as a solution to their social asset shortage.

“For us, the appeal is simple. Buying space in someone’s feed doesn’t mean you’ve earned their attention. Good creators understand what their audiences care about and how to give them something worth stopping for,” said Jared Kozel, co-founder and chief creative officer at agency Super Nice. “That’s valuable creative judgment to bring into an ad no matter the brand or category.”

Influencer marketing experts note that several different but related practices are included under the broader umbrella of creator-led production.

While some brands simply pay creators a fee in order to receive video or still assets for use in a campaign, whitelisting (also called “dark advertising”) has become a favored method of managing such arrangements.

In this context, an influencer grants a brand limited access to their social media accounts, allowing them to book a paid media campaign through that account, using assets made by the creator while taking advantage of discrete audience targeting.

“What we’re seeing is a lot of recutting of media spend to be allocated towards creator development in order to fund whitelisting,” said Olivia Wedderburn, head of influence at Born Social.

Madison & Wall’s research suggested that funding for creative production may also be coming from PR, social or experimental budgets, as well as traditional media or production pots of money.

Another related practice, user generated content, sees brands paying regular social media users to license their content as creative assets in ad campaigns.

“They have to feed their their content engines, and they’re opening up as many different avenues as they can,” said Andy Ryan, co-founder at social and influencer agency Komodo.

The relative low cost of working with influencers, versus creative production agencies, is the primary driver behind brand spending on creator-made assets.

Although production spending is often a small fraction of an overall campaign budget, marketers are keen to squeeze every non-working (that is, non-media) dollar for all it’s worth. While that same desire is pushing some brands toward generative AI production techniques, others are turning to creators.

But as this type of spending grows, so to does the need to manage it effectively. “It’s never been more complicated to negotiate usage rights or exclusivity,” said Wedderburn.

Billion Dollar Boy, for example, recently added features to its Companion creator management tool designed to better facilitate creator-led production efforts and manage usage rights negotiations.

“The creator economy has never been more competitive, heightening the urgency for brands to understand the market context,” said Thomas Walters, the agency’s chief innocation officer and co-founder.

At the same time, increased brand spending in this area is already leading to an uptick in the fees commanded by some creators. Last year, agency practitioners reported creator rates ticking up 10-20% due to demand for expanded rights.

There’s also some evidence to show that creator-made assets perform as well as, or even better than, traditional advertising spots in a social context.

A report by System1, WPP Media and Goat published in June found that creator ads achieved 3.2X the brand-awareness lift for category leader ads as traditional advertising creative.

“We’re seeing a lot of brands say that is more valuable in terms of conversion and reach than some of the quick-and-dirty assets they previously would have relied on,” said Wedderburn.

That’s not unexpected. Audiences recognize the visual cues, language and production methods employed by creators as native to TikTok or Instagram, while clocking films shot on a closed set or using more traditional methods as foreign that same environment, a lesson that major advertisers like Nike are reluctantly absorbing.

“If programs are set up correctly, creators can deliver volume and variety faster and more cost effectively than a traditional production cycle,” said Nicholas Spiro, chief commercial officer, Viral Nation. “The shift we’re seeing is brands starting to plan creators across their media budgets, rather than as a separate influencer line item alone.”

#7239. Sociable: Instagram adds Amazon affiliate links

The partnership will enable creators to add up to 30 shoppable products per Reel or 20 per feed post.

“Sociable” is the latest commentary on important social media developments and trends from industry expert Andrew Hutchinson of Social Media Today.

Instagram has added another way for creators to make money, by partnering with Amazon to enable affiliate links for Amazon-listed products in Reels and feed posts.

As shown in these example images, creators can select from a range of products on Amazon to add to their posts. Clickable links to the relevant product listings on Amazon will then be added in the bottom left of a post or Reel display, allowing viewers to easily make a purchase.

All affiliate links will be connected to the creator’s account, and creators will earn a commission for any sales generated from those referrals.

Eligible creators can link their Instagram and Amazon Influencer accounts in their Professional Dashboard on IG in order to facilitate product linking.

As per an Instagram press release sent to SMT: “Once connected, Instagram automatically includes their affiliate links when they add Amazon products to content, with product links taking viewers directly to the Amazon Shopping App.”

Instagram also said creators will be able to add up to 30 products per Reel, or 20 per feed post. This should provide a heap of linking potential for affiliate opportunities.

Creators can also see the commission rate for each item, so they’ll know how much they’ll get from any resulting link clicks.

This is another way for Instagram to provide monetization pathways for its creators, while also giving Amazon another means to promote its products via creator endorsement.

Amazon has been steadily expanding its product display opportunities, with the shopping giant also inking similar affiliate partnerships with YouTube and Pinterest this year.

Though, interestingly, Amazon asked to be removed from the list of platforms that will work with Meta’s Muse agent Amazon said that was because the Muse system was in violation of Amazon’s automated shopping tool restrictions.

A partnership with Instagram, then, seems like an interesting development, which could also lead to Amazon eventually working with Meta’s other platforms more openly.
